notes.text: For more than 8, use two loaves and cook in two skillets side by side, or keep the finished slices warm under foil while you cook more batches.

move.title: Low enough to cook the middle
move.body: Heat control means choosing how hot the pan is, and changing it when the food tells you to. Today you'll soak thick slices of challah in a sweet egg custard and cook them over medium-low heat, so the outside turns golden while the custard inside cooks all the way through.

why.title: Thick food, lower heat
why.body: Heat moves from the pan into the food slowly, from the outside in. A thin egg cooks through in a minute, but a thick slice soaked with custard needs time for the heat to reach its middle. Too hot, and the outside burns while the middle is still wet. Medium-low gives the middle time to catch up.

why.title: Dry bread drinks better
why.body: Bread a day or two old has dried out a little, so it soaks up custard like a sponge and still holds together. Fresh, soft bread soaks up too fast and falls apart. Challah is perfect because it's rich and sturdy.

why.title: Soak, don't drown
why.body: A short soak on each side gets custard into the bread without turning it to mush. Letting the extra drip off keeps puddles of raw egg out of the pan.

why.title: Butter shows the heat
why.body: Butter foams when the pan is ready. If it turns dark brown or smokes before the bread goes in, the pan is too hot. Turn it down and wipe the pan before the next batch.

wrong.fix: The pan was too hot. Turn the heat down, and give each side another minute. The thermometer tells you when the middle is done.

wrong.sign: The slices fell apart in the custard
wrong.fix: The bread was too fresh, or it soaked too long. Next batch, soak each side for just 10 seconds.

wrong.sign: Pale and soft after the timer
wrong.fix: Turn the heat up a notch and cook a minute more on each side.

wrong.sign: The butter is turning black between batches
wrong.fix: Wipe the pan with a paper towel, turn the heat down a little, and start the next batch with fresh butter.

quiz.q: Why cook French toast on medium-low instead of high?
choices: So the middle cooks before the outside burns
quiz.explain: Thick food needs time for the heat to reach the middle. Lower heat gives it that time.

quiz.q: Why is day-old challah better than fresh?
choices: It soaks up custard and still holds together
quiz.explain: Slightly dry bread drinks up the custard like a sponge without falling apart.

substitutions.note: Gluten-free bread is thinner and softer. Soak it just 10 seconds a side, and use 2 slices per person.
Use 1 tablespoon of oil in the pan for each batch.

steps.text: Cut the challah into slices about 1 inch thick, about as thick as your thumb is wide. Lay them out on the counter while you make the custard.
steps.tip: Saw gently back and forth instead of pressing down, so the loaf doesn't squash. Keep your other hand on top of the loaf, well away from the blade.

steps.text: Crack the {n:egg} eggs into the shallow dish. Add the milk, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, and {qty:salt} salt.
steps.tip: If a bit of shell falls in, scoop it out with a bigger piece of shell.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter where the eggs were.
steps.tip: Raw egg can carry germs. Clean hands before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Whisk the custard until it's smooth, with no streaks of egg white left.
steps.tip: Cinnamon likes to float on top. Keep whisking and it will mix in.

steps.text: Melt 1 tablespoon of butter in the skillet over medium-low heat until it foams.
Lay 3 or 4 slices in the custard. Soak for 20 seconds, flip them with the fork, and soak 20 seconds more. Lift each slice with the fork and let the extra drip back into the dish.
steps.tip: Use the fork, not your fingers, so your hands stay clean of raw egg.

steps.text: Lay the soaked slices in the pan. Cook until the bottoms are deep golden brown.
steps.look: Lift a corner with the spatula: deep golden, not dark brown.

steps.text: Flip each slice with the spatula and cook the second side the same way.
Slide the thermometer into the side of one slice, into the middle. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, turn the heat down a little, cook 1 more minute on each side, and check again.
steps.look: The middle springs back when you press it, with no wet custard.

steps.text: Move the slices to the plate and cover them loosely with foil to keep warm. Add another tablespoon of butter and cook the rest of the slices the same way: soak, then cook each side. Check one slice from each batch with the thermometer.
steps.tip: Whisk the custard again before each batch. The cinnamon sinks to the bottom.

steps.text: Pour out any leftover custard. Wash the dish and the fork, wipe the counter, and wash your hands with soap.
Turn off the stove. Serve the French toast warm with maple syrup.
